title: Ultra-sharp Images Make Old Stars Look Absolutely Marvelous!
caption: HP 1, imaged by the Gemini South telescope
credit: Gemini Observatory/AURA/NSF; composite image produced by Mattia Libralato of Space Telescope Science Institute.

recognition.text: Official NSF NOIRLab / Gemini press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This Gemini South image shows HP 1, and the title of its release describes the subject as old stars captured in ultra-sharp detail. It is a colour composite made with the GSAOI camera working together with the GeMS adaptive optics system, with north up and east to the left.

Stars twinkle because turbulence in Earth's atmosphere constantly bends their light, and that same turbulence blurs pictures taken from the ground. An adaptive optics system measures the distortion continually and corrects it with a flexible mirror, so a telescope on the ground can produce much sharper views than it otherwise could.

Sharpness matters especially in crowded fields of stars, where blurring can merge neighbouring stars into a single smudge; separating them lets astronomers measure each star on its own. Mattia Libralato, of the Space Telescope Science Institute, produced the composite from observations made with the Gemini South telescope in Chile.

understand.summary: Taken with the GSAOI camera and GeMS adaptive optics system on Gemini South; the filters and colour mapping aren't published.
understand.eye: Adaptive optics removes much of the atmospheric blurring that limits both telescopes and the eye, showing stars far more sharply.
